lines.cap: **Narrator:** Tuesday. Room 8H. Mr Hargreaves has reached mug twenty-two. Essay drafts are due.
**Mei:** 'Romeo climbs the wall. "But, soft! what light through yonder window breaks? It is the east, and Juliet is the sun." This shows he loves her.'
**Quotey:** OW! My serifs! You just **dropped** me onto the floor with no sentence holding me up!
**Mei:** Did... did my quotation marks just yell at me?
**Quotey:** Quotey! Golden quotation marks! I am meant to be **woven into grammar**, not dumped between full stops like abandoned luggage!
**Zoom:** Zoom. Jeweller's loupe. Worse: you copied sixteen words of Will's poetry and explained **none** of them.
**Mr H:** Retelling the plot, a **dropped quotation**, and 'this shows'. Level one, Mei.
**Will:** I wrote the greatest metaphor in Christendom, and she gave essay writing **one star**.
**Mei:** I proved he loved her! What else do they want from me?!
**Mr H:** Not **what** happens. **How** and **why**. Fetch the ladder.
**Narrator:** All the School's a Stage. Episode fifteen: Climbing the PEEL Ladder.

chapters.title: Analysis, not retelling — and your thesis

lines.cap: **Nib:** **Analysis** comes from Greek **analusis** — untying a knot — and **essay** from French **essayer**, meaning **to try** an argument.
**Mr H:** A fan says 'we scored' — that's **retelling**. A pundit explains **how** the winger dragged the defender wide — that's **analysis**.
**Will:** Take three words from **The Tempest**, Act 1 Scene 2: Caliban cries, '**This island's mine**'.
**Mr H:** **Level one** retells: 'Caliban says it's his.' **Level two** explains meaning: 'He thinks Prospero stole it.' Still no methods.
**Zoom:** **Level three** analyses method: the blunt possessive pronoun '**mine**' sounds fierce and defiant, rejecting Prospero's rule.
**Nib:** **Level four** is perceptive: in **1611**, as English ships claimed land in the Americas, '**mine**' challenges whether newcomers own what they take.
**Mei:** Okay! So I start my essay: 'In this essay I am going to write about Caliban'?
**Nib:** Never **announce**! Open with an arguable **thesis** — the one-sentence argument your whole essay proves.
**Mr H:** Use the formula: **Shakespeare presents** Caliban as both monster and victim, **in order to** make the audience question power.
**Mei:** Or use **although** for nuance: '**Although** Prospero seems wise, Shakespeare **exposes** his cruelty towards Caliban'!

chapters.title: PEEL, PETAL and embedding short quotes

lines.cap: **Mr H:** Each body paragraph climbs **PEEL**: **Point**, **Evidence**, **Explain**, **Link** — or **PETAL**, splitting Technique and Analysis.

**Will:** When Juliet cries '**My only love sprung from my only hate!**', your **Point** claims love is dangerous, **Evidence** quotes it, **Explain** unpacks the **antithesis**, and **Link** steps back to fate!
**Zoom:** Golden rule: **Explain** is the **longest** part! Milk one tiny quote for three sentences of **What, How, Why**.
**Quotey:** Which brings us to me! Remember my motto: **Snip it, slip it, unzip it!**
**Quotey:** **Snip** the quote down to **one to eight words** — only the words you will actually **unzip**!
**Mei:** Then **slip** it into my own sentence: 'Romeo's metaphor of Juliet as "**the sun**" suggests his world revolves around her'!
**Quotey:** Ooh, feel that grammar! Read it aloud without my quote marks — it flows as one smooth English sentence!
**Kevin:** Two more ways! Put a **colon** after a full clause: 'Hamlet's disgust is clear**:** Denmark is "an unweeded garden".' Or use a comma after 'he cries,'!
**Nib:** Keep quotations exact, like '**star-cross'd**'. Use a **slash** for a verse line break, **ellipsis** for cuts, and **square brackets** to adjust grammar.
**Quotey:** Like: Caliban says Prospero taught '**[him]** language'! Stylish, accurate, and zero bruised quotation marks!
**Mei:** Two stars. Snip it, slip it, unzip it is weirdly catchy.
**Narrator:** Thursday, the library. Zoom is inspecting Percy Bysshe Shelley's sonnet **Ozymandias**.
**Will:** A shattered statue in the sand wears a '**sneer of cold command**'. Good line. Wish I'd written it.
**Zoom:** **Zoom in** on one word! '**Sneer**': its **denotation** is a curling lip. Swap it for 'smile' and the tyrant vanishes!
**Mei:** Because '**sneer**' **connotes** contempt, mockery and cruelty — and the hard 'c' **alliteration** in '**cold command**' sounds barked!
**Nib:** Name the **word class** and **semantic field**: Dickens's frost, rime and ice build a semantic field of cold, while the verb '**clutching**' shows desperate greed.
**Mei:** So I write: 'This metaphor **shows** imagery and **makes the reader want to read on**'?
**Nib:** Ink emergency! Ban '**makes the reader want to read on**', '**creates imagery**' and '**paints a picture in the reader's head**'!
**Mr H:** And never **feature-spot** — 'there is alliteration here' with no effect earns almost nothing.
**Zoom:** Retire 'shows' after one use! Upgrade to **analytical verbs**: **suggests**, **implies**, **conveys**, **evokes**, **emphasises**, **exposes**, **challenges**, **foreshadows**.
**Mr H:** Notice we say '**suggests**', rarely 'proves' — because great literature invites interpretation.
**Will:** My best lines mean **two** things at once. Hamlet calls the world '**an unweeded garden / That grows to seed**'.
**Nib:** Top-band essays explore **alternative interpretations** using **tentative language**: **perhaps**, **might**, **could**, **arguably**.
**Mei:** 'The adjective "**unweeded**" **perhaps** blames Hamlet's mother for neglecting Denmark through her hasty marriage...'
**Zoom:** '**Alternatively**, it **may** point to King Claudius, suggesting corruption is choking the whole state.' Then judge which reading is stronger!
**Will:** Or when Miranda cries '**O brave new world**', she sounds hopeful — yet Prospero's dry reply, '**'Tis new to thee**', makes it ironic!
**Mr H:** Now the **L** in PEEL: link to the writer's **purpose**, **audience** and **context**.
**Mei:** Easy! 'William Shakespeare was born in **1564** in Stratford-upon-Avon and married Anne Hathaway.'
**Mr H:** Cross it out. That's **bolted-on biography** — you could paste it into any essay and it explains zero words.
**Will:** Stratford is a very relevant market town!
**Nib:** **Integrate** context into the word: for an Elizabethan audience who feared astrology, '**star-cross'd**' marked the lovers as doomed by fate from line six.

chapters.title: Comparing two texts and the PEEL showpiece

lines.cap: **Mr H:** Whole-essay architecture: **introduction** with your thesis, **logical** body paragraphs, and a deeper **conclusion** with no new quotes.
**Nib:** When **comparing two texts**, avoid writing all of Poem A then all of Poem B. Write **integrated** paragraphs comparing **methods**!
**Kevin:** Use comparative connectives! Similarity: **similarly, likewise, both**. Difference: **whereas, in contrast, while**!
**Zoom:** **Both** poets attack tyranny, **whereas** Shelley's '**sneer of cold command**' mocks one broken statue, William Blake's '**mind-forg'd manacles**' condemn mental chains across all London!
**Mr H:** Right, Mei. Final test: how does Shakespeare present Romeo's feelings in Act 2 Scene 2? Climb the ladder.
**Mei:** **Point**: Shakespeare **presents** Romeo's love as worshipful and dangerously all-consuming.
**Mei:** **Evidence**: seeing her at the window, Romeo declares that 'Juliet is **the sun**'.
**Mei:** **Explain**: the metaphor places her at the centre of his universe; '**sun**' connotes light and life, yet **perhaps** hints at sudden obsession after Rosaline.
**Mei:** **Link**: because the sun also **burns**, the image subtly **foreshadows** a blazing passion that destroys them both.
**Mr H:** Sigh... Level four, Mei. Quotey didn't even hit the floor.
**Narrator:** Friday afternoon. Room 8H's analytical survival guide.
**Mei:** Memory hooks! Paragraph shape: **PEEL** or **PETAL**. Explanation: **What, How, Why**. Quotes: **Snip it, slip it, unzip it**!
**Mr H:** One. Never **retell the plot** or open with 'In this essay I will...'. Answer straight away with an arguable **thesis**.
**Quotey:** Two. Never leave **dropped quotations** or copy four-line chunks! Weave **one to eight words** smoothly into your sentence.
**Nib:** Three. Don't **feature-spot** or write 'makes the reader want to read on'. Name the method accurately and explain its **specific effect**.
**Zoom:** Four. Swap tired 'shows' for precise **analytical verbs** — **suggests, implies, conveys, exposes** — and zoom in on **connotations**.
**Will:** Five. Use '**perhaps**' and '**alternatively**' for second readings, and **integrate** context into the words — don't bolt on my birthday.
**Kevin:** Six. Compare two texts **together** in each paragraph using **whereas**, **in contrast** and **similarly**!
**Mei:** Analytical Writing: **four stars**. Unpacking one word is way faster than copying sixteen.
**Quotey:** Four stars?! After I taught you square brackets?!
**Mei:** My hand still hurts from PEEL rung three.
**Mr H:** Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
**Mr H:** Which part of a **PEEL** paragraph should always be the **longest**?
**Zoom:** The **Explain** section — unpacking methods, connotations and effects.
**Mr H:** What does it mean to **embed** a quotation?
**Quotey:** Weaving a **short quotation** smoothly inside your own **grammatical sentence**!
**Mr H:** What is the difference between a word's **denotation** and its **connotations**?
**Nib:** **Denotation** is its dictionary meaning; **connotations** are the feelings and ideas it suggests.
**Mr H:** Which words signal an **alternative interpretation**?
**Mei:** Tentative words like **perhaps**, **might** or **could**, paired with **alternatively** or **on the other hand**.
**Mr H:** Why does writing 'Shakespeare was born in 1564' earn no context marks on its own?
**Will:** Because context must be **integrated** to explain how the **words** work on the audience, not bolted on!
**Mr H:** Brilliant work. Now try the **Analytical Writing** quiz in your English Lab.
**Quotey:** Promise you'll never drop me on the floor again?
**Mei:** Snipped, slipped and unzipped. Promise.
